column1: # scripts/harness-files.tsv: what scripts/update-harness.js does with each path the upstream ships.
# The upstream is a starting point that keeps moving, and a repo made from it has its own work in the
# same tree. This table is the line between the two: which files belong to the harness and travel, and
# which belong to the project and never do.
# The first row whose path matches wins, so the specific rows come before the general ones. A path is
# an exact file, or a prefix ending in / that matches everything under it.
#   merge  three-way merge against the upstream commit the receipt names. A file nobody touched takes
#          the new version outright; an edited one keeps its edits and gains the changes around them;
#          a real collision is written with conflict markers and reported. Created if absent.
#   reconcile as merge, and merged even when there is no receipt to take a base from: the base is
#          recovered by finding the upstream commit whose copy matches this one, and failing that the
#          file is written with conflict markers rather than left stale. For the few files nothing
#   seed   written only when it is absent, and never touched again. Scaffolding the project grows into.
#   skip   never written by an update, at all. The project's own, or generated from something else.
#   skills the vendored skill tree, which merges by name rather than by content: see update-harness.js.
#   optional:<flag> installed as seed, but only when update-harness.js is given --<flag>.
#   template the upstream’s own: never installed anywhere. Nothing a host repo runs reaches it, and shipping
#          it would leave every project carrying the machinery that maintains the upstream rather than the

column3: The project's front page. The upstream's is about the harness itself.
The project chooses its own.
Written by project-init, and the one file that says what this project is.
The loose-ends ledger, all of it the project's own.
Generated from the project's own lock file after the update, not copied.
.NET analyzer configuration. Meaningless in a repo that is not .NET, and confusing to find there.
Wiring for one agent tool. A team that does not use OpenCode would carry dead config.
The Astro site that renders the chain. Optional, and nothing in the harness reaches it: install it with --astro-docs.
The npm wrapper that publishes the installer. Whatever stack lands in a project’s src/ writes its own.
The installer. A project updates with npx @salaros/ai-harness, which clones the upstream, so it needs no copy of this.
This table. Read from the upstream checkout during an update, never from the project.
The harness suite: fixtures that prove the harness. check-edit.js skips it where it is absent.
Its fixtures.
CI that runs the suite, which does not travel either. A project brings its own.
Merged as a union, so a skill the project vendored itself survives.
Added and updated, never removed: the project may install its own.
One link to .agents/skills, not a link per skill, so every skill a repo has is visible through it -- including one written by hand that nothing vendored.
One link to .agents/agents, the same shape. Declared rather than left to the fallback, because the fallback is what a reader has to know to predict it.
Harness config the skills read. issue-tracker.md carries the project key, so it merges rather than being overwritten.
Says what the chain puts where. The artifacts under it are the project's; this file is the harness explaining the folder.
The documentation chain. Every artifact in it is the project's.
The project's code.
The project's tests.
Project tooling. The docs site lands on a first install and is then the project's to change.
Workflow specs written by loop-me, one per project.
Working notes, never shared.
The map every agent reads, and the table docs-check parses. A stale one leaves a repo that looks installed and behaves like the version it came from.
One line pointing at AGENTS.md, but a project may add to it.
Read by code-review. The upstream's is a starting set.
Crafted at the root and added to by whatever stack lands.
As above: whitespace and encoding are enforced here rather than in CODING_STANDARDS.md, so a harness change to them has to be able to reach a repo that already has one.
As above.
MCP servers: the upstream's, plus whatever the project adds.
Harness wiring for Claude Code, plus the project's own permissions.
Agents, routing and the hook scripts: the harness itself.
The Git hooks. A hook the project wrote itself is not in the upstream, so it is left alone.
The checks the Git hooks and the skills call, and the tables they read.
